body.text: In Ted Chiang's 2005 short story
“What's Expected of Us”
PDF

), the story considers what happens when people come to believe that the future is already fixed and that their choices no longer matter. I am using it here less as an argument about free will than as a warning against the passive language that often surrounds technology. We say that models will improve and governments will eventually adapt, as though these were natural events rather than the accumulated result of decisions made by companies, researchers, and institutions.

CRISPR is a useful example of how long specialized knowledge can take to accumulate. The unusual DNA sequences were first observed in bacteria in 1987, but their function was not understood at the time. It took roughly twenty-five years of work by researchers across several areas of biology before CRISPR was turned into a practical tool for editing genes. The Broad Institute’s
CRISPR Timeline
traces that development.

preview.text: , Amodei asks what becomes limiting once intelligence itself becomes much more abundant.

body.text: In
Machines of Loving Grace
, Dario points to factors such as the speed of the outside world, missing data, and human constraints in a world of abundant intelligence. In
Policy on the AI Exponential

, he makes a related policy argument for preserving optionality and improving visibility as AI capabilities change quickly. I use the two here to distinguish faster intelligence from the physical and institutional conditions needed to act on it.

body.text: Google DeepMind’s
Formal Conjectures
project is intended in part as a benchmark for automated theorem proving.

Conflict-event data offers a useful parallel because the difficulty is often not that data does not exist, but that different datasets make the world legible through different coding choices. UCDP, for example, defines state-based armed conflict through a contested incompatibility over government or territory and a threshold of at least 25 battle-related deaths in a calendar year, while ACLED collects real-time political violence and disorder events using a broader event-data structure. ACLED itself warns that care is needed when combining its data with datasets that use different units of analysis, and that findings may differ across datasets because of different scopes and methodologies.
Kristine Eck’s comparison of UCDP GED and ACLED
is useful because it shows how even adjacent, respected datasets can require substantial interpretive work before they can be responsibly compared.
The OECD’s
Cracking the Code: Rulemaking for Humans and Machines

is useful here because it shows that the need for machine-consumable public rules has already been recognized. But it should not be mistaken for the thing it describes: it is a working paper, not an implemented corpus or dataset. Its abstract presents “Rules as Code” as a proposal and describes the paper as a guide to the concept’s potential and possible public-service applications. In that sense, it also illustrates the limitation I am describing in international relations: multilateral policy institutions often identify the need for a shared structure, but do not themselves provide the structured knowledge layer it calls for.

Catala: A Programming Language for the Law

OpenFisca
is a related Rules as Code project. I use these examples not to suggest that politics can be reduced to code, but to show how structure can make translation between professional languages easier.

body.text: Scanlon's contractualism

centres on whether conduct can be justified to others while respecting their separate interests, rather than securing agreement or producing a preferred overall outcome. I borrow that distinction to claim that the worlds of policy and technology do not need to agree on everything, but the decisions they make together should be defensible to the people affected by them. They may not owe one another agreement, but they do owe one another enough openness to make their decisions defensible to the people who will live with them.
I treat
Open Weights and American AI Leadership
(July 2026) as one side of the open-weights governance debate, rather than as evidence that open weights are inherently safer.
These are the three questions posed at the beginning of the essay:

items: Who has legal or political authority?
Who controls the technology or infrastructure?
Why is there no reliable institution connecting these groups?
